cards.explanation: The recipient mounts an immune response to an antigen and can develop immunological memory.
cards.text: Vaccination induces artificially acquired {{c1::active immunity}}.
cards.question: Vaccination induces artificially acquired {{c1::active immunity}}.

cards.explanation: The aim is to establish protection before exposure causes illness.
cards.text: Vaccination given to prevent disease is described as {{c1::prophylactic}}.
cards.question: Vaccination given to prevent disease is described as {{c1::prophylactic}}.

cards.explanation: In active immunisation the recipient develops their own response, including memory cells.
cards.text: Receiving preformed protective antibodies gives {{c1::passive immunity}}.
cards.question: Receiving preformed protective antibodies gives {{c1::passive immunity}}.

cards.explanation: Other activated cells contribute to the memory pool.
cards.text: During a first response to a vaccine, some activated B cells differentiate into antibody-secreting {{c1::plasma cells}}.
cards.question: During a first response to a vaccine, some activated B cells differentiate into antibody-secreting {{c1::plasma cells}}.

cards.explanation: These include memory B and T cells.
cards.text: The cells that allow a faster antigen-specific response on re-exposure are {{c1::memory lymphocytes}}.
cards.question: The cells that allow a faster antigen-specific response on re-exposure are {{c1::memory lymphocytes}}.

cards.explanation: An IgG response follows. The horizontal axis shows time after exposure.
cards.text: In the primary-response graph, the first antibody class to rise is {{c1::IgM}}.
cards.question: In the primary-response graph, the first antibody class to rise is {{c1::IgM}}.

cards.explanation: Compare the height and speed of the second response with those of the first.
cards.text: In the lecture graph, the rapid, large antibody increase after a second exposure is dominated by {{c1::IgG}}.
cards.question: In the lecture graph, the rapid, large antibody increase after a second exposure is dominated by {{c1::IgG}}.

cards.explanation: The strength and duration of protection vary with the infection and vaccine.
cards.text: Infection-acquired immunity requires exposure to the risks of the {{c1::disease itself}}.
cards.question: Infection-acquired immunity requires exposure to the risks of the {{c1::disease itself}}.

cards.explanation: A useful response must also recognise the relevant antigen on later exposure.
cards.text: A vaccine’s capacity to elicit an immune response is called {{c1::immunogenicity}}.
cards.question: A vaccine’s capacity to elicit an immune response is called {{c1::immunogenicity}}.

cards.explanation: A strong response is useful only if it recognises a relevant target.
cards.text: If vaccine-induced antibodies bind the vaccine antigen but fail to recognise the circulating pathogen, the problem is antigenic {{c1::specificity}}.
cards.question: If vaccine-induced antibodies bind the vaccine antigen but fail to recognise the circulating pathogen, the problem is antigenic {{c1::specificity}}.

cards.explanation: Protection is not measured by antibody concentration alone.
cards.text: Alongside antibodies, vaccination can induce antigen-specific {{c1::T cells}}.
cards.question: Alongside antibodies, vaccination can induce antigen-specific {{c1::T cells}}.

cards.explanation: It is used to protect against tuberculosis, especially severe forms in children.
cards.text: BCG is an example of a {{c1::live attenuated}} vaccine.
cards.question: BCG is an example of a {{c1::live attenuated}} vaccine.

cards.explanation: This can support a strong immune response. Suitability depends on the vaccine and the recipient.
cards.text: A live attenuated vaccine can provide sustained antigen exposure because the weakened organism can {{c1::replicate}}.
cards.question: A live attenuated vaccine can provide sustained antigen exposure because the weakened organism can {{c1::replicate}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture uses this as an example of an immune response at a relevant site of exposure.
cards.text: Oral live polio vaccine can elicit immunity at the intestinal {{c1::mucosa}}.
cards.question: Oral live polio vaccine can elicit immunity at the intestinal {{c1::mucosa}}.

cards.explanation: A weakened organism can still replicate. Clinical decisions depend on the particular vaccine and patient.
cards.text: Severe immunosuppression is especially relevant when assessing eligibility for a {{c1::live}} vaccine.
cards.question: Severe immunosuppression is especially relevant when assessing eligibility for a {{c1::live}} vaccine.

cards.explanation: Antigens can still be recognised by the immune system.
cards.text: An inactivated whole-organism vaccine contains microbes that {{c1::cannot replicate}}.
cards.question: An inactivated whole-organism vaccine contains microbes that {{c1::cannot replicate}}.

cards.explanation: Preservation of the relevant epitope matters for immune recognition.
cards.text: An antibody that recognises a folded protein may lose binding when the antigen’s {{c1::three-dimensional shape}} changes.
cards.question: An antibody that recognises a folded protein may lose binding when the antigen’s {{c1::three-dimensional shape}} changes.

cards.explanation: Acellular pertussis vaccines instead contain selected antigens.
cards.text: Whole-cell pertussis vaccine is an example of an {{c1::inactivated whole-organism}} vaccine.
cards.question: Whole-cell pertussis vaccine is an example of an {{c1::inactivated whole-organism}} vaccine.

cards.explanation: The antigen does not amplify in the recipient. The schedule depends on the product.
cards.text: A non-replicating vaccine antigen may require repeated doses to maintain {{c1::protective immunity}}.
cards.question: A non-replicating vaccine antigen may require repeated doses to maintain {{c1::protective immunity}}.

cards.explanation: It retains antigenic features that allow antibodies to recognise the toxin.
cards.text: A vaccine antigen derived from an inactivated bacterial toxin is called a {{c1::toxoid}}.
cards.question: A vaccine antigen derived from an inactivated bacterial toxin is called a {{c1::toxoid}}.

cards.explanation: Their toxoid antigens induce antibodies against the disease-causing toxins.
cards.text: Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines teach the immune system to recognise bacterial {{c1::toxins}}.
cards.question: Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines teach the immune system to recognise bacterial {{c1::toxins}}.

cards.explanation: This targets toxin-mediated disease and need not prevent bacterial carriage.
cards.text: Toxoid vaccination primarily protects by inducing antibodies that {{c1::neutralise the toxin}}.
cards.question: Toxoid vaccination primarily protects by inducing antibodies that {{c1::neutralise the toxin}}.

cards.explanation: An adjuvant can strengthen responses to an otherwise weakly immunogenic antigen.
cards.text: The lecture gives {{c1::aluminium hydroxide}} as an example of an adjuvant used with a toxoid.
cards.question: The lecture gives {{c1::aluminium hydroxide}} as an example of an adjuvant used with a toxoid.

cards.explanation: An immune response can be directed against a relevant component without administering a whole organism.
cards.text: A vaccine made from selected microbial antigens is called a {{c1::subunit vaccine}}.
cards.question: A vaccine made from selected microbial antigens is called a {{c1::subunit vaccine}}.

cards.explanation: Antibodies against this surface protein can contribute to protection.
cards.text: The influenza surface protein used as an example of a subunit antigen is {{c1::haemagglutinin}}.
cards.question: The influenza surface protein used as an example of a subunit antigen is {{c1::haemagglutinin}}.

cards.explanation: Its polysaccharide is linked to a carrier protein.
cards.text: The antigen in a Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine comes from the bacterial {{c1::capsule}}.
cards.question: The antigen in a Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine comes from the bacterial {{c1::capsule}}.

cards.explanation: Purified antigens can provide a weaker stimulus on their own.
cards.text: A substance added to enhance the immune response to a vaccine antigen is an {{c1::adjuvant}}.
cards.question: A substance added to enhance the immune response to a vaccine antigen is an {{c1::adjuvant}}.

cards.explanation: Purity and the strength of the immune response are separate properties.
cards.text: A purified vaccine can be highly specific yet weakly {{c1::immunogenic}}.
cards.question: A purified vaccine can be highly specific yet weakly {{c1::immunogenic}}.

cards.explanation: The mRNA serves as a temporary template for translation.
cards.text: After mRNA vaccination, the encoded antigen is produced by the recipient’s {{c1::ribosomes}}.
cards.question: After mRNA vaccination, the encoded antigen is produced by the recipient’s {{c1::ribosomes}}.

cards.explanation: The recipient then develops an active immune response.
cards.text: An mRNA vaccine provides instructions to make an {{c1::antigen}} rather than a supply of preformed antibodies.
cards.question: An mRNA vaccine provides instructions to make an {{c1::antigen}} rather than a supply of preformed antibodies.

cards.explanation: This differs from the mRNA platform, although both expose the immune system to spike antigen.
cards.text: The Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine used an {{c1::adenoviral vector}} platform.
cards.question: The Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine used an {{c1::adenoviral vector}} platform.

cards.explanation: This process does not require alteration of the recipient’s genomic DNA.
cards.text: Vaccine mRNA is translated in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}.
cards.question: Vaccine mRNA is translated in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}.

cards.explanation: Memory lymphocytes can respond more rapidly on subsequent exposure.
cards.text: A booster dose re-exposes the immune system to antigen and recalls {{c1::immune memory}}.
cards.question: A booster dose re-exposes the immune system to antigen and recalls {{c1::immune memory}}.

cards.explanation: A later booster recalls that response.
cards.text: The first vaccine exposure that establishes immune memory is often called {{c1::priming}}.
cards.question: The first vaccine exposure that establishes immune memory is often called {{c1::priming}}.

cards.explanation: It measures coverage. Estimating effectiveness also requires health outcomes and a comparison.
cards.text: The fraction of an eligible population receiving a booster measures vaccine {{c1::uptake}}.
cards.question: The fraction of an eligible population receiving a booster measures vaccine {{c1::uptake}}.

cards.explanation: Broader coverage depends on which types are included.
cards.text: A vaccine designed to cover multiple antigenic types is {{c1::multivalent}}.
cards.question: A vaccine designed to cover multiple antigenic types is {{c1::multivalent}}.

cards.explanation: Valency describes the distinct targets in the formulation.
cards.text: A vaccine containing antigens from two variants is {{c1::bivalent}}.
cards.question: A vaccine containing antigens from two variants is {{c1::bivalent}}.

cards.explanation: Several capsular serogroups can cause invasive disease.
cards.text: The bacterium targeted by meningococcal vaccines is {{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}}.
cards.question: The bacterium targeted by meningococcal vaccines is {{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}}.

cards.explanation: Four targeted serogroups make MenACWY quadrivalent.
cards.text: A meningococcal vaccine targeting just one serogroup is {{c1::monovalent}}.
cards.question: A meningococcal vaccine targeting just one serogroup is {{c1::monovalent}}.

cards.explanation: The protein enables T-cell help for the antibody response to the polysaccharide.
cards.text: A conjugate vaccine links a capsular polysaccharide to a {{c1::carrier protein}}.
cards.question: A conjugate vaccine links a capsular polysaccharide to a {{c1::carrier protein}}.

cards.explanation: Conjugation recruits helper T-cell involvement and improves responses in young children.
cards.text: A pure polysaccharide generally elicits a weaker memory response than a {{c1::protein-conjugated polysaccharide}}.
cards.question: A pure polysaccharide generally elicits a weaker memory response than a {{c1::protein-conjugated polysaccharide}}.

cards.explanation: The carrier protein supports T-cell help.
cards.text: In a meningococcal conjugate vaccine, serogroup specificity comes from the {{c1::capsular polysaccharide}}.
cards.question: In a meningococcal conjugate vaccine, serogroup specificity comes from the {{c1::capsular polysaccharide}}.

cards.explanation: Its role here is to help generate a response against the linked polysaccharide.
cards.text: Tetanus toxoid can serve as the {{c1::carrier protein}} in a meningococcal conjugate vaccine.
cards.question: Tetanus toxoid can serve as the {{c1::carrier protein}} in a meningococcal conjugate vaccine.

cards.explanation: Serogroup B requires separate coverage.
cards.text: MenACWY covers meningococcal serogroups {{c1::A, C, W and Y}}.
cards.question: MenACWY covers meningococcal serogroups {{c1::A, C, W and Y}}.

cards.explanation: A reduction in targeted disease can be obscured by changes in other groups.
cards.text: After a serogroup-specific vaccine programme begins, surveillance should separate cases by {{c1::serogroup}}.
cards.question: After a serogroup-specific vaccine programme begins, surveillance should separate cases by {{c1::serogroup}}.

cards.explanation: Children born in different years experienced different vaccine policies.
cards.text: The Japanese MMR study compared autism diagnoses across successive birth {{c1::cohorts}}.
cards.question: The Japanese MMR study compared autism diagnoses across successive birth {{c1::cohorts}}.

cards.explanation: A cohort observed for longer has more time to receive a diagnosis.
cards.text: Following each birth cohort to the same {{c1::age}} made cumulative diagnosis proportions more comparable.
cards.question: Following each birth cohort to the same {{c1::age}} made cumulative diagnosis proportions more comparable.

cards.explanation: This observation weighs against the proposed population-level explanation. An ecological trend alone does not measure individual risk.
cards.text: If MMR uptake falls while autism diagnoses continue to rise, the two population trends move in {{c1::opposite directions}}.
cards.question: If MMR uptake falls while autism diagnoses continue to rise, the two population trends move in {{c1::opposite directions}}.

cards.explanation: The population trend did not support MMR as the explanation for the rise, consistent with wider vaccine-safety evidence.
cards.text: In the Yokohama study, autism diagnoses continued to rise after {{c1::MMR vaccination was withdrawn}}.
cards.question: In the Yokohama study, autism diagnoses continued to rise after {{c1::MMR vaccination was withdrawn}}.

cards.explanation: An apparent increase can otherwise reflect differences in how cases are detected.
cards.text: Using consistent case-finding methods over time reduces the risk of changing {{c1::ascertainment}} distorting a trend.
cards.question: Using consistent case-finding methods over time reduces the risk of changing {{c1::ascertainment}} distorting a trend.
